title: Episode 279: Muhammad Ali: The Rumble in the Jungle, the Thrilla in Manila, and the Louisville Lip
description:
The dazzling, defiant, and legendary life of Muhammad Ali: born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr., the three-time World Heavyweight Champion who revolutionized the sport of boxing and became a global symbol of moral courage, racial pride, and religious freedom. Winning Olympic gold in Rome in 1960 and dethroning the terrifying Sonny Liston in 1964, Ali proclaimed himself 'The Greatest'. When he refused induction into the United States military during the Vietnam War on religious and conscientious grounds, he was stripped of his heavyweight title, convicted of draft evasion, and banned from the ring for over three years at the peak of his physical prime. Vindicated by the Supreme Court, Ali orchestrated the most astonishing comeback in sports history, reclaiming the crown from George Foreman in the Rumble in the Jungle and surviving the brutal Thrilla in Manila against Joe Frazier. Discover the Greatest.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series celebrates the poet, warrior, and global icon whose lightning fists and unyielding moral conscience shook up the world. Here is George with the extraordinary life of Muhammad Ali.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE STOLEN RED SCHWINN AND THE ROME GOLD: 1942 TO 1960
Born in January 1942 in segregated Louisville, Kentucky, Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. was named after a nineteenth-century white abolitionist. His father Cassius Sr. was a billboard painter and musician; his mother Odessa worked as a domestic maid. When young Cassius was twelve years old, his prized red Schwinn bicycle was stolen at the Columbia Auditorium. In tears, he found Louisville police officer and boxing coach Joe Martin in a basement gym, vowing that he was going to 'whup' whoever stole his bike. Martin calmly replied: 'Well, you better learn how to fight first.' Possessing supernatural hand-eye coordination, lightning reflexes, and a relentless training ethic, young Cassius spent the next six years mastering the sweet science, fighting in six Golden Gloves tournaments. In August 1960, eighteen-year-old Cassius traveled to Rome for the Olympic Games, dancing and jabbing his way to the light-heavyweight gold medal, enchanting the international press with his radiant smile and exuberant Southern charm.  His father Cassius Clay Sr. was a frustrated artist who painted religious murals on church walls and billboards across Louisville, often lamenting to his sons that his skin color prevented him from achieving greatness in the fine arts. Joe Martin recognized in twelve-year-old Cassius a ferocious, singular obsession with conditioning: the young boy would race the city buses down Broadway on foot every morning, sprint up hills with lead weights in his shoes, and dodge rocks thrown at his head by his brother Rudolph to hone his lightning evasive head movements. In Rome, Cassius slept with his Olympic gold medal around his neck for forty-eight hours, walking through the Olympic Village with boundless charisma, signing autographs for fans in half a dozen languages.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE LOUISVILLE LIP AND DETHRONING SONNY LISTON: 1960 TO 1964
Turning professional under the financial sponsorship of eleven prominent Louisville businessmen, Clay developed a revolutionary boxing style that defied all traditional heavyweight orthodoxy. Heavyweights were expected to plant their feet and trade devastating blows; Clay danced on his toes, kept his hands at his waist, and pulled his head back to slip punches by fractions of an inch, composing rhythmic poetry to predict the exact round his opponents would fall. He dubbed himself 'The Louisville Lip', reciting rhymes: 'Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee; your hands can't hit what your eyes can't see.' On February 25, 1964, twenty-two-year-old Clay faced the terrifying, underworld-connected World Heavyweight Champion Sonny Liston in Miami Beach as a seven-to-one underdog. Taunting Liston as a 'big ugly bear', Clay completely outclassed the champion with blinding speed. When Liston failed to answer the bell for the seventh round, Clay leapt to the ropes, screaming at the stunned ringside press: 'I shook up the world! I am the greatest!'  Sonny Liston was widely regarded by boxing experts as an invincible, hulking mob-connected enforcer whose iron jab and bone-crushing left hook had destroyed former champion Floyd Patterson in barely two minutes. Clay's audacious psychological warfare was a tactical masterstroke designed to rattle Liston's composure: he drove a bus painted with the words 'Sonny Liston Is Dead' to Liston's training camp in Denver, shouting insults through a megaphone at two o'clock in the morning. In the ring, Clay's lateral footwork was a revelation: he circled away from Liston's lethal left hook, peppering the scowling champion with blinding jabs until Liston's eyes were swollen shut and his left shoulder tendon was torn from throwing wild, missed punches into empty air.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: MUHAMMAD ALI AND THE VIETNAM CRUCIBLE: 1964 TO 1967
The morning after defeating Liston, Clay announced that he had joined the Nation of Islam, rejecting his birth name as a slave name and adopting the name Muhammad Ali, bestowed by religious leader Elijah Muhammad. The announcement stunned white America, triggering furious condemnation from sports journalists and boxing promoters. Ali defended his heavyweight crown nine times with dazzling virtuosity, including his immortal three-minute destruction of Cleveland Williams in November 1966. But in April 1967, summoned to the military induction center in Houston, Texas, Ali refused to step forward when his name was called for the military draft, citing his religious beliefs as a Muslim minister. Ali uttered the electrifying declaration that echoed around the globe: 'I ain't got no quarrel with them Viet Cong. No Viet Cong ever called me nigger.' Indicted by an all-white jury, sentenced to five years in federal prison, and stripped of his heavyweight championship belt and boxing licenses worldwide, Ali was exiled from the ring at the absolute height of his athletic prime.  Ali's embrace of the Nation of Islam and his close intellectual friendship with Malcolm X alienated the traditional white sporting establishment, who viewed his rejection of Christianity and his new Islamic name as an act of intolerable rebellion. Defending his heavyweight crown against all challengers, Ali dazzled audiences with his unprecedented hand speed, firing hundreds of jabs and combinations without ever taking a step backward or absorbing a solid counterpunch. His refusal to step forward for the draft in Houston in April 1967 was an act of supreme moral sacrifice: he was immediately stripped of his title by the World Boxing Association before he had even been indicted in a court of law, facing the loss of millions of dollars in future fight purses and five years of imprisonment.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE WILDERNESS YEARS AND THE SUPREME COURT VINDICATION: 1967 TO 1971
From age twenty-five to twenty-eight—years when most heavyweight champions reach the pinnacle of their physical power—Ali was forbidden to box anywhere on earth. Facing financial ruin, federal surveillance, and public vitriol, Ali toured American university campuses, speaking to packed auditoriums of college students about racial justice, Black pride, anti-war morality, and human rights. As the Vietnam War grew increasingly unpopular and public consciousness shifted, Ali was transformed from a reviled pariah into a heroic countercultural prophet of moral principle. In 1970, with the assistance of Atlanta state senator Leroy Johnson, Ali was granted a boxing license in Georgia, returning to the ring to stop Jerry Quarry. In June 1971, in the landmark unanimous ruling Clay v. United States, the Supreme Court of the United States overturned Ali's conviction, affirming his conscientious objector status and fully vindicating his sacrifice.  During his exile from the ring, Ali was subjected to constant FBI wiretaps and harassment by federal authorities, yet he refused every lucrative offer to stage covert exhibition bouts overseas or sign back-channel compromises with military recruiters. Touring colleges across the United States, Ali spoke with mesmerizing rhetorical power to predominantly white student audiences, explaining that true courage lay not in dropping napalm on Vietnamese villagers, but in standing up for justice, brotherhood, and human dignity at home. In June 1971, the Supreme Court issued a unanimous eight-to-zero decision in Clay v. United States, ruling that the Department of Justice had improperly misled the draft board regarding the sincere religious foundation of Ali's pacifist Muslim beliefs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FIGHT OF THE CENTURY AND THE FRAZIER RIVALRY: 1971 TO 1974
On March 8, 1971, Ali stepped into the ring at Madison Square Garden against undefeated World Heavyweight Champion 'Smokin' Joe' Frazier in 'The Fight of the Century'. It was a clash of titans watched by hundreds of millions worldwide: Frazier's bobbing, relentless body assault against Ali's dazzling combinations and foot speed. In the fifteenth round, Frazier landed a thunderous left hook that deposited Ali on the canvas; though Ali leaped to his feet in seconds, Frazier was awarded the unanimous decision, handing Ali the first professional defeat of his career. Undaunted, Ali fought a relentless campaign of contenders, avenging his defeat against Frazier in a 1974 rematch and earning the right to challenge the terrifying, undefeated young monster who had destroyed Frazier in two rounds: George Foreman.  The atmospheric intensity surrounding the March 8, 1971 showdown at Madison Square Garden was unprecedented in sporting history, drawing Hollywood celebrities, world leaders, and underworld figures who paid thousands of dollars for ringside seats. Ali and Frazier fought at a blistering, breathless pace for fifteen grueling rounds: Frazier relentlessly slipped Ali's stinging jabs to deliver vicious left hooks to the ribs, while Ali fired dazzling three-punch combinations into Frazier's swollen face. In the climactic fifteenth round, Frazier unleashed a devastating leaping left hook that exploded against Ali's jaw, sending Ali sprawling onto his back in an immortal image of human ferocity, though Ali's instant rise from the canvas proved his superhuman resilience.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE RUMBLE IN THE JUNGLE: KINSHASA 1974
On October 30, 1974, in Kinshasa, Zaire, thirty-two-year-old Ali faced twenty-five-year-old Foreman in the 'Rumble in the Jungle', promoted by Don King. Foreman was a fearsome knockout artist who had destroyed forty consecutive opponents; commentators openly feared Ali would be maimed or killed. Before sixty thousand African fans chanting 'Ali, boma ye!'—Ali, kill him!—Ali unveiled his audacious secret strategy: the 'Rope-a-Dope'. Leaning back against the loose ring ropes, shielding his head with his gloves, Ali absorbed Foreman's bone-crushing power punches for seven exhausting rounds in the equatorial heat, taunting the champion: 'Is that all you got, George?' By the eighth round, Foreman was completely spent and arm-weary. Seizing the moment, Ali pushed off the ropes, unleasing a lightning five-punch combination crowned by a straight right hand that sent Foreman crashing to the canvas. In one of the greatest upsets in sporting history, Muhammad Ali had reclaimed the World Heavyweight Championship.  George Foreman entered the ring in Kinshasa possessing a terrifying aura of physical invincibility, having knocked down Frazier six times in two rounds and demolished Ken Norton with equal ferocity. Ali's trainer Angelo Dundee had noticed that the tropical heat and high humidity would rapidly dehydrate a heavy puncher, leading Ali to deliberately rest on the loose ropes during the early rounds, leaning his torso beyond the boundary of the ring to absorb Foreman's clubbing blows on his padded forearms and shoulders. As Foreman's punches grew slower and his chest heaved for breath under the African night sky, Ali began launching blistering right-hand leads over Foreman's lowered guard, culminating in the dazzling eighth-round combination that deposited the giant face-down on the canvas.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE THRILLA IN MANILA, PARKINSON'S, AND THE ETERNAL CHAMPION
In October 1975, Ali and Joe Frazier met for the final time in the stifling, one-hundred-degree heat of the Philippine Coliseum in the 'Thrilla in Manila'. It was the most brutal, punishing war in heavyweight history, a primal test of human endurance that Ali described as 'the closest thing to dying that I know of'. When Frazier's trainer Eddie Futch halted the bout before the fifteenth round due to Frazier's swollen, shut eyes, Ali collapsed to the canvas in utter exhaustion, retaining his crown. Ali became the first man to win the heavyweight championship three distinct times by outpointing Leon Spinks in 1978. Diagnosed with Parkinson's syndrome in 1984, the silenced warrior touched the heart of the world at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, holding the Olympic torch with trembling hands to ignite the cauldron before billions of weeping viewers. Muhammad Ali passed away in June 2016 at age seventy-four, forever remembered not merely as the greatest boxer who ever lived, but as a fearless champion of the human spirit who sacrificed everything for his principles.  The third clash between Ali and Frazier in Manila pushed both men beyond the limits of biological endurance, as temperatures inside the un-airconditioned arena soared past one hundred and ten degrees Fahrenheit. Both men absorbed hundreds of flush head punches in a horrifying war of attrition, trading murderous blows until both fighters were hallucinating from dehydration and physical trauma. In his later life, as Parkinson's syndrome robbed him of his physical agility and silver voice, Ali's gentle spirit and boundless love for ordinary people transformed him into a universal ambassador of peace, visiting orphanages, securing the release of American hostages in Iraq, and reminding the world that true greatness is measured by love, humility, and compassion.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Muhammad Ali's extraordinary speed, moral bravery, and magnetic charisma redefined the power of an athlete to impact global culture. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the roaring legend of Babe Ruth, the Sultan of Swat who created the modern American sporting spectacle. Until then, stay curious.
